summary: Describes SCRAM, a family of SASL and GSS-API mechanisms that let clients prove they know a password without sending it in the clear. It aims to fix problems that kept earlier challenge-response mechanisms from being widely deployed. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You show you know a secret by answering a puzzle that only someone who knows it could answer, without ever saying the secret out loud.

subtitle: A password login that proves you know the password without ever sending it, and also lets you check the server.

tldr.problem: Sending a clear-text password over a TLS-protected channel is the most widely used secure login, but it has security concerns. The challenge-response mechanisms then on the standards track were too hard to deploy widely.
tldr.mechanism: SCRAM is a family of SASL mechanisms. The client and server swap random nonces, the server supplies a salt and an iteration count, and the client sends a proof built from the password. The server answers with its own signature, so each side checks the other.
tldr.outcome: SCRAM-SHA-1 became the mandatory-to-implement member of the family. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 7677 and RFC 9266.

today: RFC 5802 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7677 and RFC 9266, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why SCRAM Exists
sections.content:
The abstract starts from a plain observation: the most widely deployed secure authentication on the Internet is sending a clear-text password over a channel protected by Transport Layer Security (TLS). A challenge-response mechanism running inside TLS would address the security concerns with that approach, but the challenge-response mechanisms on the standards track at the time failed the requirements for wide deployment.

RFC 5802 defines the Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM), a family of mechanisms for the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL, RFC 4422). It is also a mechanism for the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), because it conforms to the GS2 bridge between the two.

The listed features are: the stored authentication information is not enough by itself to impersonate the client, and it is salted against pre-stored dictionary attacks; the server cannot impersonate the client to other servers (with an exception for server-authorized proxies); mutual authentication is supported, but only the client is named; and SASL authorization identities can be carried.

For simplicity, SCRAM does not negotiate a security layer. It is meant to run under an external one such as TLS or SSH, with optional channel binding.
sections.eli5: Showing your password to a guard works only if nobody is listening. SCRAM is a way to prove you know the password while nobody learns what it is.

sections.title: The Algorithm in Brief
sections.content:
The client starts with a username and password and sends the username. The server looks up the user's authentication information: a salt, an iteration count i, a StoredKey and a ServerKey. It sends the salt and the iteration count back.

The client then computes a chain of values. SaltedPassword is Hi(Normalize(password), salt, i), where Hi is essentially PBKDF2 with HMAC as the pseudorandom function. From it come ClientKey and ServerKey, each an HMAC over a fixed string ("Client Key" and "Server Key"). StoredKey is the hash of ClientKey. The client signs the whole exchange (the AuthMessage) with StoredKey to get a ClientSignature, and sends ClientProof, which is ClientKey XOR ClientSignature.

The server computes the same ClientSignature, XORs it with the proof to recover ClientKey, hashes that, and compares it to its StoredKey. A match proves the client has access to the password. In the other direction the server sends a ServerSignature, and the client compares it to its own value. A match proves the server had access to the user's ServerKey.

Both the username and the password MUST be encoded in UTF-8, and the password is normalized with the SASLprep profile of stringprep (implementations MUST either implement SASLprep or disallow non-ASCII codepoints).
sections.eli5: The server keeps a scrambled version of your secret, not the secret itself. You do a calculation that only works if you know the real secret, and the server checks your answer against the scrambled version.

sections.title: The Four-Message Exchange
sections.content:
SCRAM is a client-first SASL mechanism whose messages are text, made of comma-separated attribute-value pairs. Each attribute has a one-letter, case-sensitive name. The server's final message carries data along with the successful outcome.

  1. client-first-message: a GS2 header (a channel binding flag and an optional authorization identity), the username n and a random client nonce r. The message always starts with n, y or p; anything else MUST fail authentication.
  2. server-first-message: the client nonce with the server's own nonce appended, the salt s and the iteration count i.
  3. client-final-message: the channel binding data c, the same combined nonce and the client proof p.
  4. server-final-message: the server signature v, or an error e.

The client MUST check that the start of the nonce is the one it sent, and the server MUST check that the nonce in the third message is the one it sent in the second. If the server signature does not match, the client MUST treat the exchange as failed. For SCRAM-SHA-1, servers SHOULD announce an iteration count of at least 4096.

The optional a attribute carries an authorization identity, for example when an administrator acts on behalf of another user. The m attribute is reserved for mandatory extensions, and in this version its presence MUST cause authentication failure. Unknown optional extensions MUST be ignored. Section 7 gives the formal ABNF, including the list of server error values such as invalid-proof and unknown-user.
sections.eli5: It is a four-step conversation. You say who you are, they give you a puzzle, you answer it, and they answer a puzzle of yours to prove they are the real server.

sections.title: Mechanism Names and Channel Binding
sections.content:
A SCRAM mechanism name is SCRAM-, then the uppercased name of the hash function from the IANA "Hash Function Textual Names" registry, then optionally -PLUS. SASL mechanism names are limited to 20 octets, so hash names longer than 9 octets need a shorter alternative name. All SCRAM clients and servers MUST implement SCRAM-SHA-1.

The -PLUS suffix means the server supports channel binding: tying the authentication to the external secure channel (such as TLS) underneath it. A server that supports it SHOULD advertise both the plain and the PLUS name. The client's choice is signalled by a flag in the first message: n (no channel binding support), y (the client supports it but thinks the server does not) or p= followed by the binding type (the client requires it).

If a server sees y but does support channel binding, it MUST fail authentication, because that suggests a downgrade attack in which an attacker removed the PLUS name from the server's list. The server MUST always validate the client's c= field.

The default channel binding type is tls-unique. Servers that implement any channel binding MUST implement it, and clients SHOULD.
sections.eli5: Channel binding is like checking that the person on the phone is calling from the same room you are in. It stops a middleman from quietly passing your answers along to the real server.

sections.title: SCRAM as a GSS-API Mechanism
sections.content:
The same messages also work as a GSS-API mechanism. Differences: the GS2 header and channel binding data are left out of the client's first message, and the initial context token header from RFC 2743 is added in front of it. The RFC notes that this section is informational for SASL implementors and normative for GSS-API implementors.

The mechanism OID for SCRAM-SHA-1 is 1.3.6.1.5.5.14. Security contexts always have mutual authentication set to true and credential delegation set to false. Initiators use the single name type GSS_C_NT_USER_NAME. Per-message tokens follow the Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism, and the 128-bit session key is derived from the least significant 128 bits of an HMAC over the stored key, client key and authentication message.
sections.eli5: The same secret-proving trick can be plugged into two different kinds of sockets, and this part explains the second socket.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without a strong security layer such as TLS with confidentiality, a passive eavesdropper learns enough to mount an offline dictionary or brute-force attack on the password. How long that takes depends on the hash, the password strength and the iteration count.

If the authentication database is stolen, the same offline attack is possible, and salt helps by forcing a separate attack on each password. Worse, an attacker who has the stored information and either watches one exchange or impersonates a server can impersonate that user to all servers using the same hash function, password, iteration count and salt, so salts should be randomly generated. The working group chose not to base SCRAM on EKE-like mechanisms, which resist the stolen-database attack.

Other points the RFC makes: SCRAM does not negotiate a hash function (SASL mechanism negotiation does); it provides no security layer, so protecting mechanism negotiation needs channel binding or an external channel that authenticates the server name; it does not protect against downgrade of channel binding types; and a hostile server can send a huge iteration count to burn client CPU.
sections.eli5: The scrambled secret is only safe if the thief cannot guess quickly. Salt and a high iteration count make every guess slow and force a thief to start over for each person.

sections.title: Why Not the Older Mechanisms
sections.content:
The appendices explain the motivation. DIGEST-MD5 proved too complex to implement and test, so interoperability is poor, and its security layer is rarely used because everyone uses TLS. CRAM-MD5 is widely deployed but lacks internationalized usernames and passwords, authorization identity passing, channel binding and server authentication. PLAIN lets a malicious server or eavesdropper impersonate the user to any other server with the same password, sends the password in the clear without TLS, and has no server authentication.

SCRAM's stated design goals include all the modern SASL features, mutual authentication, stored data that cannot impersonate the client, and being easier to implement than DIGEST-MD5.
sections.eli5: The older ways of logging in each had a flaw, like being too complicated or letting the wrong person copy your key. SCRAM tries to fix those flaws.
